title: Your vendor's model is your regulatory obligation
linkedinPost:
23% of organisations still don't monitor which AI models their vendors are running. The EU AI Act just made that their regulatory problem.

EU AI Act Article 26 is live. Enforcement began August 2025.

The rule is simple: if you deploy a high-risk AI system — credit decisions, onboarding, fraud scoring — the compliance obligation is yours. Even when the model is someone else's.

Most fintech vendor contracts were written before this existed. They contain:
• No model transparency clause ("AI-powered" is not a disclosure)
• No right to audit the vendor's compliance evidence
• No incident notification SLA that fits DORA's 4-hour window

What I would actually do:

• Run a vendor contract audit this quarter — not a security scan, a model disclosure review
• Add model name, version, and training data scope as non-waivable procurement requirements
• Negotiate an explicit audit rights clause, referencing Article 26
• Test whether your vendor notification SLAs actually fit your DORA reporting window
• File your own conformity assessment — a vendor's trust document is not a deployer assessment

Third-party breach costs average $4.91M (Secureframe, 2025). Most of that cost is not the breach. It is the absence of documentation.

The gap between compliant and exposed almost always lives in the contract.

Full piece + the Vendor Model Accountability Test I use to diagnose where contracts fall short — link in comments.

mainEntity.name: What does EU AI Act Article 26 require from AI system deployers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Deployers of high-risk AI systems must conduct due diligence on their AI providers, ensure the system is used as intended, maintain qualified human oversight, and document their conformity assessment. This obligation applies whether the model is built in-house or supplied by a vendor. Enforcement began August 2025 for general-purpose AI model providers.

mainEntity.name: Is my company responsible for my AI vendor's compliance failures?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under EU AI Act Article 26, yes — unless the contract explicitly shifts liability to the vendor through indemnity clauses covering regulatory penalties arising from the provider's model failures. The default assumption in EU law is that the deployer is responsible for what their deployed system does. Vendor selection and ongoing oversight are part of that responsibility.

mainEntity.name: What should an AI vendor contract include for financial services compliance in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: At minimum: model disclosure (name, version, training data scope), a right to audit compliance evidence with 30 days' notice, a change notification period of at least 30 days before material model updates, an incident notification SLA of 2 hours or less for model-affecting events, and indemnity covering regulatory penalties arising from the vendor's model failures. The European Commission MCC-AI template (updated March 2025) is the public reference document.

mainEntity.name: How does DORA affect AI vendor contracts in financial services?

acceptedAnswer.text: DORA requires ICT incidents affecting critical functions to be reported to regulators within 4 hours. If a vendor's AI model is involved in that incident and your contract contains no incident notification clause, you may receive vendor notification too late to meet the reporting window. DORA's TLPT requirements also extend to critical third-party ICT providers — which increasingly include AI vendors. Ensure your vendor contracts specify a notification SLA materially shorter than your DORA reporting window.
